points.t: Lets the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issue construction permits, operating licenses, combined licenses and amendments without a hearing.
Requires 30 days notice of its intent, published once in the Federal Register.
Limits any hearing the Commission does hold under this subparagraph to informal adjudicatory procedures.
Applies to all applications and proceedings pending before the Commission on or after enactment.

points.t: Allows construction of a uranium enrichment facility to begin before its license is issued, on the same terms as other fuel cycle facilities.
Requires an applicant to certify that it will notify the Governor, local governments and certain Tribes in writing at least 15 days before construction starts.
Keeps the Commission's authority to deny a license for failure to meet regulatory requirements; NEPA, hearing rights and inspections are unaffected.
Gives the Commission 180 days after enactment to issue or revise regulations.

text: (a) IN GENERAL.—Section 193 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2243) is amended—
(1) by striking subsections (a) through (c) and inserting the following:
“(a) AT-RISK CONSTRUCTION.—

“(1) IN GENERAL.—Construction of a uranium enrichment facility prior to the issuance of a license under sections 53 and 63 for that facility shall be permitted under the same terms and conditions applicable to other fuel cycle facilities licensed under those sections.

“(2) RULE OF CONSTRUCTION.—Paragraph (1) may not be construed to modify the licensing and regulatory authority of the Commission to issue a license under sections 53 and 63 for a uranium enrichment facility, including the authority to deny an application for such a license for the failure of an applicant to meet regulatory requirements.”; and
(2) by redesignating subsections (d) through (f) as subsections (b) through (d), respectively.

(b) NOTIFICATION OF ENRICHMENT CONSTRUCTION.— As part of an application for a license under sections 53 and 63 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2073, 2093) for operation of a uranium enrichment facility, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (referred to in this section as the “Commission”) shall require that an applicant submit a certification that, not fewer than 15 days before commencing construction of the uranium enrichment facility pursuant to subsection (a) of section 193 of that Act (42 U.S.C. 2243), the applicant will submit a written notification with respect to commencing construction to—
(1) the Governor of the State in which the uranium enrichment facility is to be located;
(2) the chief executive and governing body of each unit of local government in which the facility is to be located; and

(3) the governing body of each Indian Tribe with an offsite response organization that would be notified by the applicant in the event of an emergency, as described in the emergency plan of the applicant pursuant to section 70.22(i)(3)(viii) of title 10, Code of Federal Regulations (or a successor regulation), if applicable.

(c) REGULATIONS REQUIRED.—Not later than 180 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the Commission shall issue or revise regulations to carry out this section and the amendments made by this section.
(d) RULE OF CONSTRUCTION.—None of the amendments made by this section shall be construed to affect—

(1) the applicability of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq.) to the issuance of a license under section 53 or 63 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2073, 2093) for a uranium enrichment facility;
(2) the right of any person whose interest may be affected by a proceeding under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2011 et seq.) to a hearing under section 189 of that Act (42 U.S.C. 2239); or
(3) the authority of the Commission to conduct inspections of uranium enrichment facilities.

points.t: Treats prescribed fire as an exceptional event for Clean Air Act air quality monitoring data; the term includes cultural burning as an Indian tribe determines.
Deems a State petition for an exceptional event approved if EPA does not act within 1 year, unless the Administrator later determines it is not one.
Gives the Administrator 270 days after enactment to propose revisions to the exceptional-event regulations and 180 more days to finalize them.
Allows competitive grants with a federal share of up to 90 percent for assessing and controlling wildfire smoke hazards in community buildings, including schools.
Caps at 25 percent the share of each year's grant funds going to recipients in one State.

text: (a) AIR QUALITY MONITORING DATA INFLUENCED BY EXCEPTIONAL EVENTS.—

“(A) EXCEPTIONAL EVENT.—
“(i) IN GENERAL.—The term ‘exceptional event’ means an event—
“(I)(aa) that—

“(BB) is not reasonably controllable or preventable; and

“(aa) determined by the Administrator, through the process established in the regulations revised under paragraph (2)(B), to be an exceptional event; or

(b) SMOKE READY COMMUNITIES PROGRAM.—

(1) ESTABLISHMENT.—Subject to the availability of appropriations, the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (referred to in this subsection as the “Administrator”) may make competitive grants under section 103(b)(3) of the Clean Air Act (42 U.S.C. 7403(b)(3)) to eligible entities for the assessment, prevention, control, or abatement of wildfire smoke hazards in community buildings, including school buildings (as defined in section 11 of the Asbestos School Hazard Detection and Control Act of 1980 (20 U.S.C. 3610)), and related activities.

“(C) BROWNFIELDS INVENTORY.—Each State or Indian tribe receiving a grant under this subsection shall maintain, update not less than annually, and make available to the public, by location, an inventory of all brownfield sites within that State on which activities authorized and funded pursuant to that grant have occurred.”; and
(2) in paragraph (3), by striking “subsection $50,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2019 through 2023.” and inserting the following: “subsection—
“(A) $60,000,000 for fiscal year 2027;
“(B) $65,000,000 for fiscal year 2028;
“(C) $70,000,000 for fiscal year 2029;
“(D) $75,000,000 for fiscal year 2030; and
“(E) $80,000,000 for fiscal year 2031.”.
(c) STUDIES, REPORTS, AND GUIDANCE.—

(1) CAPITALIZATION OF REVOLVING LOAN FUNDS STUDY.—Not later than September 30, 2028, the Comptroller General of the United States shall submit to Congress a report containing a review of revolving loan funds that were capitalized using a grant received under subparagraph (A)(i) of section 104(k)(3) of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (42 U.S.C. 9604(k)(3)) during any of fiscal years 2015 through 2025, including information on—
(A) the status and balance of each such revolving loan fund;
(B) each loan or grant provided by an eligible entity under subparagraph (B) of that section; and
(C) any barriers to the eligible entity providing additional loans or grants under that subparagraph.
(2) REPORT ON FUNDING FOR COVERED ENTITIES AND COVERED APPLICANTS.—
(A) IN GENERAL.—Not later than September 30, 2030, the Administrator shall submit to Congress a report on—

(i) the effect of providing a grant under clause (ii) of section 104(k)(7)(A) of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (42 U.S.C. 9604(k)(7)(A)) (as amended by subsection (a)(6));
(ii) the covered applicants selected by the Administrator under that clause; and
(iii) the status of—
(I) any applications for a grant under section 104(k) of that Act (42 U.S.C. 9604(k)) submitted by a covered applicant that received technical assistance pursuant to that clause; and
(II) any activities for which a grant was provided pursuant to such an application.
(B) UPDATED REPORT.—Not later than September 30, 2032, the Administrator shall submit to Congress an update to the report submitted under subparagraph (A).
(3) REPORT ON LOAN PROGRAMS FOR ASSESSMENT, REMEDIATION, AND REUSE OF BROWNFIELD SITES.—

(A) IN GENERAL.—Not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of this Act, the Administrator shall submit to the Committee on Energy and Commerce of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Environment and Public Works of the Senate a report containing—

(i) an analysis of whether establishing and implementing a loan program for the assessment, remediation, and reuse of brownfield sites, consistent with section 104(k) of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (42 U.S.C. 9604(k)), would be feasible and useful, including consideration of—
(I) the demand for larger loans for which the amount of the loan is equal to or greater than the largest loan currently offered by eligible entities under paragraph (3)(B) of that section;
(II) the extent to which such a program would facilitate the remediation and reuse of brownfield sites at which potential contamination is particularly extensive or complex; and
(III) the extent to which such a program could facilitate the remediation and reuse of 1 or more brownfield sites at an earlier date than such activities would otherwise proceed; and
(ii) if the Administrator finds such a program will be feasible and useful, recommendations for statutory changes needed to authorize such a program.

(B) CONSULTATION.—In carrying out this paragraph, the Administrator shall consult with other Federal agencies, eligible entities, site owners, site developers, and any other entities the Administrator considers appropriate.

(4) NATIONAL PRIORITIES LIST DELETION STUDY.—The Comptroller General of the United States shall conduct a study with respect to the process for the deletion or partial deletion of sites from the National Priorities List established under section 105 of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (42 U.S.C. 9605) in order to identify any barriers to such deletion or partial deletion, including a review of the following:
(A) The process of coordination between Federal and State entities with respect to that deletion or partial deletion.
(B) Any impediments to timely and efficient deletion or partial deletion of sites.
(C) Opportunities to expedite the deletion or partial deletion of sites with respect to which applicable remedial action has been completed.
(5) GUIDANCE FOR PERMITTING ON BROWNFIELD SITES.—

(A) IN GENERAL.—Not later than 1 year after the date of enactment of this Act, the Administrator shall develop guidance to assist Federal agencies in more efficiently issuing Federal authorizations, and conducting environmental reviews for such authorizations, with respect to projects relating to brownfield sites.
(B) CONSIDERATIONS.—In developing or updating guidance under this paragraph, the Administrator shall consider matters related to—
(i) the availability of historic site-specific environmental data;
(ii) previously completed environmental reviews required by the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq.);

(iii) data or information collected as part of assessment or remediation activities under section 104(k) of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (42 U.S.C. 9604(k));
(iv) community engagement and historical experience with previous uses; and
(v) any other matters the Administrator determines appropriate.
(C) UPDATES.—The Administrator shall update the guidance developed under this paragraph periodically.
(6) DEFINITIONS.—In this subsection:
(A) ADMINISTRATOR.—The term “Administrator” means the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency.
(B) BROWNFIELD SITE.—The term “brownfield site” has the meaning given the term in section 101 of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (42 U.S.C. 9601).
(C) FEDERAL AUTHORIZATION.—The term “Federal authorization”, with respect to a project—
(i) means any authorization required under Federal law for the project; and
(ii) includes any permits, special use authorizations, certifications, opinions, or other approvals as may be required under Federal law for such project.
(D) REMEDIAL ACTION.—The term “remedial action” has the meaning given the term in section 101 of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (42 U.S.C. 9601).

text: (a) DEFINITIONS.—In this section:
(1) COMPUTATIONAL LOAD SITE.—
(A) IN GENERAL.—The term “computational load site” means 1 or more buildings, structures, or installations at a single location that primarily contain information technology infrastructure used for—
(i) creating, executing, and delivering software applications and services;
(ii) artificial intelligence training, deployment, and delivery;
(iii) cryptocurrency mining; or
(iv) other computational activities at a data center.

(B) EXCLUSION.—The term “computational load site” does not include computing or data storage equipment that is ancillary to a facility the primary purpose of which is a commercial or industrial activity other than an activity described in subparagraph (A).
(2) PROGRAM.—The term “program” means the Data Center Community Assistance Program established under subsection (b)(1).
(3) SECRETARY.—The term “Secretary” means the Secretary of Energy.
(b) DATA CENTER COMMUNITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM.—

(1) IN GENERAL.—Not later than 180 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the Secretary shall establish a program, to be known as the “Data Center Community Assistance Program”, under which the Secretary shall provide State, local, and Tribal governments, on request, with objective and technically sound information, resources, and technical assistance regarding the potential energy, water, infrastructure, economic, and other community impacts associated with computational load site development.
(2) COMMUNITY TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE.—Assistance by the Secretary under the program may include providing information and analysis relating to—
(A) projected electricity demand, including peak and annual demand;
(B) existing electric generation, transmission, and distribution capacity and any additional infrastructure needed to serve the computational load site;
(C) anticipated costs of electric infrastructure upgrades, including which persons are expected to pay those costs, and potential impacts on other ratepayers;
(D) projected water withdrawals and consumption, including average and peak water use;
(E) proposed water sources and the relationship between projected use and available local water supplies;
(F) proposed cooling technologies and associated energy and water requirements, including potential alternative technologies;
(G) backup and onsite generation, including capacity, fuel source, and anticipated use;
(H) expected economic impacts, including construction jobs, permanent jobs, and other employment effects;
(I) anticipated State and local tax revenues and any tax abatements, credits, grants, infrastructure assistance, or other public incentives;
(J) suggested information for communities to request from computational load site developers, electric utilities, water utilities, and other relevant entities;

(K) information and examples from similarly situated communities, including agreements, infrastructure arrangements, resource-use practices, and other approaches to computational load site development; and
(L) other relevant information relating to the potential energy, water, infrastructure, and economic impacts of computational load site development.
(c) DATA CENTER COMMUNITY TOOLKIT.—

(1) IN GENERAL.—Not later than 180 days after the date of enactment of this Act, the Secretary shall develop a Data Center Community Toolkit, which shall be publicly accessible and specifically written for nontechnical local officials in plain English.
(2) CONTENTS.—The Data Center Community Toolkit developed under paragraph (1) shall include—
(A) model questions to ask computational load site developers and utilities, including questions relating to infrastructure costs;
(B) explanations or definitions, as applicable, of the terms “megawatt”, “megawatt-hours”, “power usage effectiveness”, and
“water usage effectiveness”;
(C) examples of cooling systems;
(D) explanations of utility rate structures;
(E) case studies from other communities relating to computational load site development; and
(F) a guide to potential benefits and tradeoffs of hosting a computational load site.
(d) INDEPENDENT PROJECT ANALYSIS.—
(1) IN GENERAL.—At the request of a State, local, or Tribal government, the Secretary may—

(A) request the applicable computational load site developer to voluntarily provide to the Secretary information, data, analyses, models, assumptions, estimates, projections, and other materials relating to the proposed computational load site; and
(B) independently assess that information and those materials, including by evaluating—
(i) the reasonableness of the assumptions and methodologies used;
(ii) the reliability of the data;
(iii) whether estimates and projections are adequately supported by the information provided; and
(iv) the technical reasonableness of the conclusions reached.

(2) TIMELINESS.—The Secretary shall make every reasonable effort to provide information and analysis under paragraph (1)(B) in a timely manner, taking into consideration the timeline of the applicable State, local, or Tribal government for consideration of the proposed computational load site.
(e) NEUTRALITY.—In carrying out activities under this section, the Secretary—
(1) shall clearly identify material assumptions, limitations, and uncertainties associated with any analysis provided; and

(2) shall not make any recommendation to a State, local, or Tribal government regarding whether any particular computational load site should be approved, rejected, permitted, or otherwise authorized.
(f) RULES OF CONSTRUCTION.—Nothing in this Act—

(1) authorizes the Secretary to approve, disapprove, condition, delay, or otherwise participate in a State, local, or Tribal decision regarding the siting or development of a computational load site; or

(2) limits the authority of the Secretary under any other provision of law to provide financial assistance, including grants, loans, loan guarantees, or other assistance, for a project or to an entity associated with a computational load site.
sponsor_summary: Adds S. 5645, which establishes a Data Center Community Assistance Program at the Department of Energy to provide State, local, and Tribal governments, on request, with technical assistance on the potential energy, water, infrastructure, economic, and other community impacts associated with data center development (Curtis/Blunt Rochester).

points.t: Requires the Secretary of Energy to announce any alteration of a directive or safety standard for a covered DOE nuclear facility within 72 hours, with a summary.

Applies the same 72 hours to issuing a preliminary or final documented safety analysis; the announcement includes the analysis, redacted only for commercially sensitive, classified or controlled information.
Adds a third announcement, due within 72 hours of entering an agreement to authorize a covered DOE nuclear facility, that lists any conditions in the agreement.

Sets January 31 each year as the date for the Secretary to report to the House Energy and Commerce and Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committees on the prior calendar year's authorization activities.

text: (a) ALTERATIONS TO DIRECTIVES AND SAFETY STANDARDS.—

(1) PUBLIC ANNOUNCEMENT.—Not later than 72 hours after altering a directive or safety standard relating to covered DOE nuclear facilities, the Secretary of Energy shall post, on a publicly accessible website of the Department of Energy, an announcement regarding such alteration.
(2) INCLUSION.—Each announcement under paragraph (1) shall include a summary of how the relevant directive or safety standard was altered.
(b) DOCUMENTED SAFETY ANALYSIS.—

(1) PUBLIC ANNOUNCEMENT.—Not later than 72 hours after issuing any preliminary documented safety analysis or documented safety analysis with respect to a covered DOE nuclear facility, the Secretary of Energy shall post, on a publicly accessible website of the Department of Energy, an announcement regarding the issuance of such preliminary documented safety analysis or documented safety analysis.
(2) INCLUSION.—
(A) ANALYSIS.—Subject to subparagraph (B), each announcement under paragraph (1) shall include the relevant preliminary documented safety analysis or documented safety analysis.

(B) COMMERCIALLY SENSITIVE OR CONTROLLED INFORMATION.—The Secretary of Energy may modify a preliminary documented safety analysis or documented safety analysis included in an announcement under paragraph (1) only to ensure that such preliminary documented safety analysis or documented safety analysis does not include any commercially sensitive information, classified information, unclassified controlled nuclear information, or controlled unclassified information.

(c) AUTHORIZATIONS.—Not later than 72 hours after entering into an agreement to authorize a covered DOE nuclear facility, the Secretary of Energy shall post, on a publicly accessible website of the Department of Energy, an announcement regarding such agreement, including information regarding any conditions applying to such agreement.

(d) REPORT.—Not later than January 31 of each year, the Secretary of Energy shall submit to the Committee on Energy and Commerce of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources of the Senate a report detailing any activities the Secretary of Energy took to authorize covered DOE nuclear facilities during the previous calendar year.
(e) DEFINITIONS.—In this section:

(1) COVERED DOE NUCLEAR FACILITY.—The term “covered DOE nuclear facility” means any of the Hazard Category 1, 2, and 3 DOE nuclear facilities (as such term is defined in section 830.3(a) of title 10, Code of Federal Regulations (or a successor regulation)) that the Secretary of Energy holds authority over pursuant to section 110 a. of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2140(a)).

(2) DOCUMENTED SAFETY ANALYSIS; PRELIMINARY DOCUMENTED SAFETY ANALYSIS.—The terms “documented safety analysis” and “preliminary documented safety analysis” have the meanings given such terms, respectively, in section 830.3(a) of title 10, Code of Federal Regulations (or a successor regulation).

points.t: Omits the definition of “property of traditional religious or cultural importance” in section 302706(a). Was: a place where an event of continuing religious or cultural significance to a living community occurred.

Drops the rule that the Secretary assumes the functions of a Tribal Historic Preservation Officer when a tribal program stays inconsistent after 2 years. Was: the Secretary took over all or part of those functions.

Requires a written determination, technical assistance and at least 180 days to submit a corrective action plan before the Secretary disapproves a tribal program or suspends its agreements. Was: no such steps.
Adds a process to reinstate a tribal program and restore eligibility for suspended contracts, agreements and grants. Was: no such process.

Covers each undertaking with a 60-day report on its area of potential effects, historic properties and adverse effects, sent to start consultation. Was: a report only when the agency found adverse effects.
Gives State and Tribal Historic Preservation Officers, Tribes and other consulting parties 45 days to submit substantive objections before the agency proceeds. Was: 30 days.
Accepts any substantive comment other than a form letter as the comment a claimant needs. Was: a substantive and unique comment.
Sets a schedule of no more than 90 days for the agency to act when a court finds it missed its consultation deadline. Was: injunctive relief with no stated deadline.
Caps the time for the court to decide at 120 days after the complaint, absent extraordinary circumstances. Was: as expeditiously as practicable.
Removes projects receiving more than $10,000,000 from the Department of Transportation from the exclusion for projects with only financial assistance. Was: the exclusion applied to all such projects.
Limits the repair exclusion to “minor or routine” work. Was: “minor” work.

sponsor_summary: Strikes the definition of property of traditional religious or cultural importance.
Requires written notice to a tribe if the Secretary of the Interior finds a Tribal Historic Preservation Office (THPO) program is not in compliance with program requirements.
Strikes the provision requiring the Secretary of the Interior to assume the duties of a THPO if a THPO program is not compliant.
Adds a provision allowing non-compliant THPOs to use a corrective action process to bring the program into compliance.
Delays any withholding of grants or other funding to THPOs until two years of continued non-compliance with program requirements after implementation of a corrective action plan.
Clarifies that THPO program compliance activities do not relieve any agency of the requirement to consult with an Indian tribe under 302706(b) of the National Historic Preservation Act.
Requires the Department of the Interior to provide technical assistance, training, and support to THPOs.
Clarifies that Federal Highway Administration projects are subject to section 106 requirements even if the only federal nexus for the project is a formula grant implemented by a state.
Adds additional allowance for “routine” projects to be excluded from section 106 consideration if they do not diminish the historic integrity of a historic property.

Codifies in statute the current regulatory language that excludes from section 106 review undertakings that are of a type of activity that does not have the potential to cause adverse effects on historic properties.
Adds a requirement that, if an undertaking is governed by a program alternative, the agency shall proceed in accordance with the program alternative.

Expands original requirement that the federal agency considering the undertaking solicit information, discuss that information, and incorporate that information into a report on the area of potential effects and the identification of historic properties with the area of potential effects, to now also include whether there are any adverse effects on those historic properties. The federal agency must prepare a report including those elements and incorporating information from SHPOS, THPOs, Indian tribes, Native Hawaiian organizations, local governments, and project, activity, or program applicants.

Requires consultation with SHPOS, THPOs, Indian tribes, Native Hawaiian organizations, local governments, and project, activity, or program applicants on the report, including the area of potential effect, the identification of historic properties, the determination of adverse effects, and any actions to avoid, minimize, or mitigate those adverse effects.
Removes the requirement for SHPOs and THPOs to spend 50 percent of their time on a specific project if a deadline is missed.
Adds deadlines for courts to act on complaints related to a federal agency missing section 106 deadlines.
Extends the deadline from 30 days to 45 days for substantive objections to be provided after the report is provided to consulting parties.
Removes the provision allowing the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation to consult or sign an agreement in lieu of an Indian tribe or Native Hawaiian Organization.

When there is both a federal and state or Tribal programmatic agreement governing an undertaking, allows the SHPO or THPO to choose the federal programmatic agreement over the state or Tribal programmatic agreement.
Removes requirement for comments to be “unique” to establish standing. Replaces it with language that excludes form letter comments from establishing standing.

points.t: Excludes from gross income, under Internal Revenue Code section 104(a)(2), damages received on account of any sexual act or sexual contact, with or without medical records or observable injuries.

Treats a statement in a decision or agreement that damages are on account of a sexual act or contact as credible evidence, and treats the taxpayer as meeting the substantiation requirement of section 7491(a)(2).
Applies to amounts received under decisions made, and agreements entered into, after enactment.
Counts an agreement that replaces, supersedes or revises an earlier agreement as not entered into after enactment.
Directs the Secretary of the Treasury, with the Justice Department Office on Violence Against Women, to run a program promoting public awareness of the exclusion.

text: (a) IN GENERAL.—Section 104(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 is amended by striking “on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness;” and inserting “on account of—
“(A) personal physical injuries or physical sickness, or

“(B) any sexual act (as defined in paragraph (2) of section 2246 of title 18, United States Code, as in effect on the date of the enactment of this subparagraph) or sexual contact (as defined in paragraph (3) of such section, as so in effect), whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries of such act or contact;”.

(b) BURDEN OF PROOF WITH RESPECT TO WHETHER DAMAGES ARE ON ACCOUNT OF SEXUAL ACT OR SEXUAL CONTACT.—Section 104 of such Code is amended by redesignating subsection (d) as subsection (e) and by inserting after subsection (c) the following new subsection:

“(d) BURDEN OF PROOF WITH RESPECT TO WHETHER DAMAGES ARE ON ACCOUNT OF SEXUAL ACT OR SEXUAL CONTACT.—For purposes of subsection (a)(2), if a decision or agreement states that any damages received therefrom are on account of a sexual act or sexual contact referred to in subsection (a)(2)(B)—
“(1) such statement shall be treated as credible evidence that such damages are so on account for purposes of section 7491(a), and
“(2) the taxpayer shall be treated as having met the requirements of section 7491(a)(2) with respect to the issue of whether such damages are so on account.”.
(c) EFFECTIVE DATE.—
(1) IN GENERAL.—The amendments made by this section shall apply to amounts received pursuant to decisions made, and agreements entered into, after the date of the enactment of this Act.

(2) SPECIAL RULE FOR DECISIONS.—For purposes of paragraph (1), a decision shall be treated as made after the date of the enactment of this Act if the first payment pursuant to such decision is received after such date.

(3) SPECIAL RULE FOR AGREEMENTS.—For purposes of paragraph (1), an agreement shall not be treated as entered into after the date of the enactment of this Act if such agreement replaces, supersedes, or revises an agreement entered into on or before such date.

(d) NO INFERENCE WITH RESPECT TO EFFECT OF MEDICAL RECORDS OR OBSERVABLE INJURIES ON DETERMINATIONS WITH RESPECT TO PERSONAL PHYSICAL INJURIES OR PHYSICAL SICKNESS.—No inference may be drawn from the amendment made by subsection (a) (or from section 104(a)(2)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended by subsection (a)) with respect to whether the term “personal physical injuries or physical sickness” as used in section 104(a)(2) of such Code includes injuries or sickness with respect to which there are no medical records or observable injuries.

(e) PROMOTION OF PUBLIC AWARENESS OF EXCLUSION.— The Secretary of the Treasury (or the Secretary’s delegate), in consultation with the Department of Justice Office on Violence Against Women and other relevant Federal agencies, shall conduct a program to promote public awareness of the exclusion from gross income provided by section 104(a)(2)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended by this section.

highlights.label: Data center costs
highlights.t: Drops the 20-megawatt floor for data center load by replacing “covered load” with computational load owners, operators and sites. Was: rules applied only to load of 20 megawatts or more.

highlights.label: Permit certainty
highlights.t: Lets agencies act on any federal court order or under any applicable law. Was: only where a court required it.

highlights.label: Disparate-treatment suits
highlights.t: Counts the 10 most recent calendar years of denial and delay data. Was: the 5 most recent.

highlights.label: Historic preservation and Tribes
highlights.t: Omits the definition of “property of traditional religious or cultural importance” in section 302706(a). Was: a place where an event of continuing religious or cultural significance to a living community occurred.

highlights.label: Tribal preservation offices
highlights.t: Drops the rule that the Secretary assumes the functions of a Tribal Historic Preservation Officer when a tribal program stays inconsistent after 2 years. Was: the Secretary took over all or part of those functions.

highlights.label: Clean Water Act certification
highlights.t: Drops consistency with the Federal license or permit from the tests certification conditions must meet. Was: a third test, alongside necessity and least burden.

highlights.label: Where NEPA suits are heard
highlights.t: Sends claims challenging a federal agency's NEPA rule, or an authorization for a project with no physical location, only to the D.C. Circuit. Was: the circuit where the project would be built or run.

highlights.label: Consolidated grid planning
highlights.t: Applies the consolidated planning rule to each Transmission Organization. Was: each transmission planning region.

highlights.label: Behind-the-meter resources
highlights.t: Limits qualifying behind-the-meter resources to a rated capacity of 5 kilowatts to 5 megawatts. Was: 5 kilowatts or more, with no upper limit.

highlights.label: Help for communities weighing data centers
highlights.t: Directs the Secretary of Energy to set up a Data Center Community Assistance Program within 180 days of enactment.

highlights.label: Nuclear licensing hearings
highlights.t: Lets the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issue construction permits, operating licenses, combined licenses and amendments without a hearing.

highlights.label: Brownfields funding
highlights.t: Authorizes $200,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for the brownfields grant and loan program.
